record_reviews.observation: Reeks explicitly forwards answers to Darwin’s questions and a Liebig bone extract. The enclosure answers each numbered specimen: 1312/1313 salts, 763 sodium sulphate, 1633 mixed salts, 1227 calcium chloride, 3048 neither anhydrite nor gypsum, 759/762 no cause for curing failure, and bone 25 at about 7 percent animal matter and 8 percent water.

exact_evidence.quote: I have great pleasure in forwarding the answers to your questions, together with the extract upon bones from Liebig.
You will observe in No. 1313 that there is but a very little Carbonate of Lime, which appears to me strange, as, in No. 1312, a continuation of the same bed, there is an abundance.

record_reviews.observation: Reeks encloses the quantitative analysis of salt 759: 99.52 sodium chloride, 0.26 calcium sulphate and 0.22 earthy matter, concluding it cannot explain the salt’s inferiority and withdrawing his prior potassium suspicion.

exact_evidence.quote: I have much pleasure in enclosing you a copy of the analysis of the Salt (No 759.) I can find nothing in it to account for its inferiority and my former suspicion of its being Potassium proves groundless.
I am, Dear Sir | Your obedient Servt. | Trenham Reeks C Darwin Esqre. Analysis of Salt (No. 759) from Patagonia. Chloride of Sodium— 99.52 Sulphate of Lime 0.26 Earthy matter 0.22 —– 100.00 —–

record_reviews.observation: Reeks reports Kane’s account of d’Arcet’s failed soda manufacture: damp mixtures of calcium carbonate and common salt can produce some sodium carbonate, but only in small quantities. Phillips reports the examined rock contains only traces of calcium sulphate.
